source.title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions

accepted.question_text: Are the statistical properties predicted by the time-reversal-invariant Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) consistent with experimental data on compound-nucleus resonances strongly enough to justify using random-matrix theory as a physically meaningful tool in nuclear reaction theory, including tests based on resonance spacings, widths, and quantum-number-clean resonance sequences?
accepted.context_brief: GOE consistency with compound-nucleus resonance data

evidence.quote: The question has two parts. (i) Are the properties predicted by the GOE consistent with experimental data on CN resonances? (ii) Is it possible to implement the GOE into a viable and useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions? An affirmative answer to question (i) is the neccessary condition for a physically meaningful use of RMT in nuclear reaction theory.
In general, the data agree with GOE predictions. Open questions exist for the ∆3 statistic for long sequences of levels, and for the distribution of neutron widths.

accepted.question_text: Can the GOE be implemented as a viable and useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions whose theoretically predicted observables are broad enough for practical nuclear-reaction applications, rather than being limited to too narrow a set of quantities?

evidence.quote: The question has two parts. (i) Are the properties predicted by the GOE consistent with experimental data on CN resonances? (ii) Is it possible to implement the GOE into a viable and useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions?
The range of theoretically predicted observables has grown in recent years but is still too narrow. Theoretical expressions for cross-section correlation functions would be particularly valuable.

accepted.question_text: For the nuclear dynamics relevant to applying the GOE in nuclear reaction theory, is the underlying dynamics chaotic in the sense needed for random-matrix spectral-fluctuation predictions to apply, given the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture that systems chaotic in the classical limit have spectral fluctuations agreeing with random-matrix theory?
accepted.context_brief: Chaotic nuclear dynamics as GOE premise

evidence.quote: According to the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture [12], the spectral fluctuation properties of dynamical systems that are chaotic in the classical limit agree with RMT predictions. Therefore, the applicability of the GOE to nuclear reaction theory is linked to the question whether the nuclear dynamics is chaotic.

accepted.question_text: In shell-model calculations for s-d-shell nuclei with spin J = 2 and isospin T = 0 states near the middle of the shell, why does the Mehta-Dyson ∆3 statistic tend to lie slightly above the GOE prediction for very large sequence lengths L even though both the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution and the ∆3 statistic otherwise agree very well with GOE predictions?

evidence.quote: Both the NNS distribution and the ∆3 statistic were calculated for the 3276 states with spin J = 2 and isospin T = 0 that occur in the middle of the shell. In both cases, agreement with the GOE is very good, except that the ∆3 statistic has a tendency to lie slightly above the GOE curve for very large lengths L. That tendency seems not fully understood.

accepted.question_text: Do shell-model configurations and compound-nucleus resonances at excitation energies lying midway between two major nuclear shells exhibit the mixing and spectral-fluctuation behavior expected from the GOE, or does the GOE expectation established within a single major shell fail or change in that between-shell regime?

evidence.quote: To be sure, the mixing addressed in Ref. [13] refers only to the configurations within a single major shell. Shell structure being manifest over a wide range of excitation energies, one may wonder what happens at excitation energies that lie in the middle between two major shells. That question seems not to have been addressed in the theoretical literature.

accepted.question_text: How can low-energy neutron-scattering analyses cleanly separate s-wave neutron resonances from p-wave resonances, including resonances of unknown parity or known p-wave character, so that conclusions about GOE spectral statistics and neutron-width distributions are firm and unbiased?
accepted.context_brief: Separating s-wave and p-wave neutron resonances

evidence.quote: One cause of uncertainty in the data analysis described so far is due to the possible presence of p-wave resonances in low-energy neutron scattering data. It is clear that firm and unbiased conclusions can only be drawn if s-wave and p-wave neutron resonances are cleanly separated.
As in the case of the level distribution, it is important to ascertain that all levels included in the analysis are s-wave resonances.

accepted.question_text: For the reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble, is the reported disagreement between the ∆3 statistic and the GOE prediction at sequence lengths L > 20 a genuine rejection of the GOE hypothesis, or can it be explained by effects such as too few long sequences, underestimated statistical uncertainty, experimentally missed narrow resonances at increasing distance from neutron threshold, or erroneous p-wave assignments among excluded resonances?

evidence.quote: However, for the remaining nuclei in the reconstructed NDE (U and Th nuclei omitted) the ∆3 statistic deviates increasingly with increasing length L from the GOE prediction, the deviation becoming significant for lengths L > 20 or so.

Given these facts we are left with the disagreement with GOE predictions found in Ref. [7] for the ∆3 statistic and for sequence lengths L > 20. Here several questions come to mind. (i) Table I of Ref. [6] shows that the number of sequences with L > 20 decreases strongly with increasing L. Estimates of the statistical uncertainty of the ∆3 statistic in Ref. [7] do not seem to reflect that fact. (ii) It is known that with increasing distance from neutron threshold, an increasing number of narrow resonances is missed experimentally.
An erroneus p-wave assignment to the excluded resonances seems to offer the most likely explanation.

accepted.question_text: Do neutron widths of isolated compound-nucleus resonances follow the Porter-Thomas distribution predicted by the GOE, or do the small and widely spread maximum-likelihood estimates of the chi-squared degree-of-freedom parameter ν in Pt nuclei and reconstructed-NDE analyses remain inconsistent with the GOE after accounting for cutoff choice, finite sample size, and simulation-calibrated uncertainty in the maximum-likelihood method?

evidence.quote: The conclusions in Refs. [5, 6] are based on the ML analysis with a cutoff. How reliable is that method?
In the light of these results, it is not clear whether the two small ν values found in Ref. [5] are inconsistent with the GOE.
It appears that definite conclusions on the validity of the GOE hypothesis can be drawn only when every ML analysis using a cutoff is supported by simulations of the type used in Ref. [22].
The case of neutron widths [5, 6] is unresolved.

accepted.question_text: How can the standard GOE scattering formulation with a fixed number Λ of open channels and an energy-independent coupling matrix W be given an adequate theoretical treatment for experimentally relevant s-wave neutron channels, where neither an angular-momentum barrier nor a Coulomb barrier suppresses coupling to GOE states and the fixed-channel approximation over a finite energy interval can be most strongly violated?
accepted.context_brief: s-wave neutron channels in GOE scattering theory

evidence.quote: The number Λ of open channels in Eqs. (4, 5) is considered fixed. With increasing energy, the number of open channels in any nuclear reaction actually increases exponentially. Therefore, Eqs. (4, 5) provide a useful approximation to S only within some finite energy interval ∆E.

The assumption is most strongly violated by s-wave neutron channels because here neither angular momentum barrier nor Coulomb barrier suppress the coupling to the GOE states. It seems that the number of such cases that are experimentally relevant, is small. Their adequate theoretical treatment would pose a problem.

accepted.question_text: Can one derive practically useful GOE/RMT predictions beyond average cross sections and beyond the Ericson regime, especially theoretical expressions for cross-section correlation functions, when existing analytical results are limited to two-S-matrix-element correlations, selected three- and four-element cases, single-element distributions, and the complete joint distribution only for strongly overlapping resonances?
accepted.context_brief: Cross-section correlation functions beyond Ericson regime

evidence.quote: Because of the technical difficulties in the calculation of such averages, the predictive power of the GOE for nuclear reactions is actually much more limited than for spectral fluctuations.

General analytical results exist only for the correlation function involving a pair of S-matrix elements [23], for select values of the correlation function involving three or four S-matrix elements [24, 25], and for the probability distribution of single S-matrix elements [26, 27, 28, 29]. The complete joint probability distribution of all S-matrix elements is known [30, 31, 32] only in the Ericson regime (strongly overlapping resonances). From a practical point of view, results beyond average cross sections and beyond the Ericson regime, especially for cross-section correlation functions, would be of considerable interest.
Theoretical expressions for cross-section correlation functions would be particularly valuable.

trace.notes: Resolved arXiv abs URL to the arXiv PDF, downloaded it, and mapped the PDF title, abstract, Sections 1-5, acknowledgments, and references over pages 1-10.
Section 1 explicitly states the two-part framing question: GOE consistency with CN resonance data and GOE implementation as a viable reaction theory.
Section 2 links GOE applicability to the question whether nuclear dynamics is chaotic.
Section 3.1 identifies an unexplained large-L ∆3 tendency in shell-model calculations and asks what happens between major shells.
Section 3.1 isolates p-wave admixture and the reconstructed-NDE ∆3 disagreement for L > 20 as candidate unresolved issues.
Section 3.2 presents unresolved neutron-width PTD/GOE tests and uncertainty in cutoff-based maximum-likelihood analyses.
Section 4 identifies theoretical-treatment limits for s-wave neutron channels and missing GOE predictions for cross-section correlation functions beyond the Ericson regime.
Expanded CN, RMT, and GOE context from Section 1 while keeping the question focused on experimental justification of the GOE approach.
Expanded the implementation question with the source-supported limitation that the range of predicted observables remains too narrow.
Rewrote the chaos premise as a standalone applicability question using the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit conjecture evidence.
Restated the unexplained ∆3 excess with its shell-model setting, quantum numbers, and large-L condition.
Restated the between-major-shell question and inlined the single-major-shell limitation.
Converted the source's stated need for clean s-wave/p-wave separation into a standalone methodological research challenge.
Combined the reconstructed-NDE L > 20 ∆3 discrepancy with the source-listed possible explanations.
Combined neutron-width PTD status with source-supported ML cutoff, finite-sample, and simulation-calibration issues.
Expanded the s-wave neutron-channel implementation issue with the fixed-channel and energy-independent-W assumptions stated in Section 4.
Expanded the missing-observable problem with the explicitly listed limits of existing analytical GOE S-matrix results.

No near-duplicate candidates were merged. The broad framing questions q_001 and q_002 were retained separately from narrower subproblems because the source explicitly states them as the two parts of the overarching problem.
